title: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — Section 21 (Award of Lok Adalat)

content.overview: Section 21 treats a Lok Adalat award as a civil-court decree or, as the case may be, an order of another court. It provides for court-fee refund on settlement of a case referred under section 20(1), and makes the award final and binding on the parties with no appeal to any court.
content.glance: Section 21(1): deemed decree or other-court order, plus refund for a settled section 20(1) case. Section 21(2): final and binding award; no statutory appeal to any court.
content.study: Section 21(1) has two distinct consequences. First, every Lok Adalat award is deemed a decree of a civil court or, where applicable, an order of another court. Second, where the Lok Adalat reaches a compromise or settlement in a case referred under section 20(1), court-fee paid in that case is refunded in the manner provided under the Court-fees Act, 1870. The refund limb must not be described as an automatic refund for every ADR process or every pre-litigation application. Section 21(2) makes every Lok Adalat award final and binding on all parties to the dispute and excludes an appeal to any court against it. Section 20 separately governs referral, settlement efforts and the consequences of failure; a failed reference must not be presented as a settlement award under section 21. The statutory no-appeal rule does not by itself resolve every possible constitutional or exceptional challenge; any such proposition requires separate authoritative case-law review. This account is based on the NALSA Act PDF; full current-law, case-law and PDF legibility review remain open.

sections.heading: Operative rule
sections.body: Separate the award's deemed-decree/other-court-order status, the conditional court-fee refund in section 21(1), and finality plus no appeal in section 21(2). Check that an award actually exists rather than assuming one from referral alone.

provisions.title: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — Section 21 (Award of Lok Adalat)

examTips: Use three headings: legal status of award; court-fee refund for a settled section 20(1) case; finality and no appeal. Do not infer total immunity from every form of judicial scrutiny.

learningObjectives: Explain deemed-decree or other-court-order status under section 21(1).
Apply the section 20(1) settlement condition to court-fee refund.
State finality and the no-appeal rule without inventing a judicial-review test.
enhancement.definition: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 — Section 21 (Award of Lok Adalat)
enhancement.legalPrinciple: An actual Lok Adalat award attracts the statutory decree/order effect and finality rules. The court-fee refund limb specifically concerns compromise or settlement of a case referred under section 20(1).
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, sections 20 and 21(1)-(2); Court-fees Act, 1870 for the refund manner expressly referenced in section 21(1).
essentialIngredients: An award made by a Lok Adalat, not merely a reference or unsuccessful settlement attempt.
Deemed status as a civil-court decree or, where applicable, an order of another court.
For refund, compromise or settlement in a case referred under section 20(1) and court-fee paid in that case.
Finality and binding effect on all parties to the dispute, with no appeal to any court against the award.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 21(1) should not be reduced to civil-decree status alone: it also mentions an order of another court and specifies a conditional refund. Identify the case's reference under section 20(1), the settlement and court-fee payment before applying the refund limb. Section 21(2) then supplies finality, binding effect and no appeal. Keep those statutory consequences separate from unreviewed propositions about execution procedure, constitutional review or exceptional challenges.
examples: Hypothetical: a pending suit referred under section 20(1) settles before the Lok Adalat. Identify the resulting award's decree/order effect and consider the court-fee refund limb in section 21(1).
Hypothetical: parties fail to settle a pre-litigation reference. Apply section 20(6), not section 21 finality, because the facts identify no settlement award.
problemApplication: Establish that an award exists and identify the parties bound by it.
Separate decree/order status from the refund conditions; identify a section 20(1) reference and paid court-fee before discussing refund.
State the no-appeal rule exactly; do not substitute an arbitral-award challenge procedure or an unverified constitutional-review test.
keyTakeaways: Section 21(1) includes both a civil-court decree and, where applicable, an order of another court.
The refund limb is tied to settlement of a case referred under section 20(1).
No appeal is a statutory rule; broader challenge propositions require separately reviewed authority.

distinctions.title: Award effect versus conditional court-fee refund
distinctions.right: Refund for a settled court-referred case

rows.left: An award attracts deemed-decree/other-court-order status and the section 21(2) finality/no-appeal rule.
rows.right: The refund limb requires compromise or settlement in a case referred under section 20(1); apply the manner referenced in section 21(1).

rows.left: Referral without settlement is not an award merely because the file reached a Lok Adalat.
rows.right: Do not extend this refund statement to every pre-litigation matter or other ADR procedure.

shortAnswer.prompt: What are the distinct effects of section 21?
shortAnswer.answer: An award is deemed a civil-court decree or, where applicable, an order of another court. Section 21(1) also provides court-fee refund for settlement in a section 20(1) case. Under section 21(2), the award is final and binding on the parties and no appeal lies to any court.
shortAnswer.method: Separate award status, conditional refund and finality.

tenMark.application: Distinguish the settlement award from a reference returned without settlement under section 20.

State section 21(2) finality and binding effect on the parties, and its no-appeal rule, without inventing an alternative challenge test.

sixteenMark.application: Identify whether the reference produced an award; distinguish the statutory response to failure from the effects of a successful settlement award.
Apply both limbs of the decree/other-court-order formulation rather than describing the award only as a private agreement.

sixteenMark.application: Trace the reference to section 20(1), identify compromise or settlement and paid court-fee, and use the statute's specified refund manner.
Use section 21(2) for the parties to the dispute and distinguish a statutory appeal from separately researched judicial-review questions.
